questions.title: How exactly does the partition function cancel in the DPO Bradley–Terry reparameterization?
questions.question_body:
In Section 4, the paper substitutes the optimal policy form into the Bradley–Terry (BT) model and claims the partition function term cancels when computing preference probabilities. Concretely, starting from

p^*(y_1 \succ y_2 \mid x) = \sigma(r^*(x,y_1) - r^*(x,y_2)),

and the reparameterization

r^*(x,y) = \beta \log \frac{\pi^*(y \mid x)}{\pi_{\text{ref}}(y \mid x)} + \beta \log Z(x),

how do we algebraically show that the \(\beta \log Z(x)\) terms vanish and obtain Eq. (7)? A line-by-line derivation would help me see why no approximation is used here.

questions.title: Deriving the closed-form optimal policy for KL-regularized RLHF objective (Eq. 5)
questions.question_body:
The paper states that the solution to

\max_{\pi} \; \mathbb{E}_{y \sim \pi(\cdot \mid x)}[r(x,y)] - \beta \mathbb{D}_{\mathrm{KL}}[\pi(\cdot \mid x) \| \pi_{\text{ref}}(\cdot \mid x)]

is

\pi_r(y \mid x) \propto \pi_{\text{ref}}(y \mid x) \exp\big(r(x,y)/\beta\big).

Could someone provide the precise derivation using calculus of variations or Lagrange multipliers, including how normalization is enforced and under what conditions on the support (e.g., what if \(\pi_{\text{ref}}(y \mid x)=0\) for some \(y\))?

questions.title: What does the DPO gradient weighting term mean, and why does the naive ratio objective “degenerate”?
questions.question_body: Eq. (9) shows the DPO gradient is weighted by \(\sigma(\hat r_\theta(x,y_l) - \hat r_\theta(x,y_w))\). Intuitively, this upweights examples where the model currently prefers the loser. Why would removing this weighting (i.e., pushing up \(y_w\) and down \(y_l\) uniformly) lead to degeneration of the language model? Is there a simple example that shows how unweighted negative training collapses diversity or causes over-confidence?

questions.title: Is DPO just supervised fine-tuning on preferred outputs with an added KL term?
questions.question_body: At first glance, Eq. (8) looks like maximizing the likelihood of \(y_w\) and minimizing the likelihood of \(y_l\) relative to a reference via a log-ratio. Is DPO equivalent to MLE on \(y_w\) with a KL penalty to \(\pi_{\text{ref}}\)? If not, what is the key difference in the objective and its optimization dynamics compared to standard supervised fine-tuning plus KL regularization?

questions.title: How should we choose and interpret the DPO temperature parameter \(\beta\)?
questions.question_body: DPO uses \(\beta\) both in the reparameterized reward \(\hat r_\theta = \beta \log(\pi_\theta/\pi_{\text{ref}})\) and inside the logistic in Eq. (8). How should \(\beta\) be selected in practice? What are the effects of scaling \(\beta\) up or down on (a) the effective strength of the KL constraint, (b) optimization stability, and (c) the reward–KL frontier? Is \(\beta\) identifiable, or can it be absorbed into a rescaling of the implicit reward without changing the optimum?

questions.title: Sequence-level vs token-level log-probabilities in DPO: how to handle length bias?
questions.question_body: Eq. (8) uses \(\log \pi(y \mid x)\), but for language models we usually decompose \(\log \pi(y \mid x) = \sum_t \log \pi(y_t \mid x, y_{<t})\). If two candidates \(y_w\) and \(y_l\) have different lengths, this introduces a length effect. Should we normalize by length (e.g., average per token) or use a length penalty in DPO? How did the authors compute these terms in practice, and what happens if we change that choice?

questions.title: What happens if the reference model assigns zero probability to some tokens or sequences?
questions.question_body: The implicit reward is \(\hat r_\theta(x,y) = \beta \log \frac{\pi_\theta(y \mid x)}{\pi_{\text{ref}}(y \mid x)}\). If \(\pi_{\text{ref}}(y \mid x) = 0\) (or numerically underflows), the log-ratio is undefined. How is this handled in DPO implementations? Does this imply we must ensure support inclusion \(\mathrm{supp}(\pi_\theta) \subseteq \mathrm{supp}(\pi_{\text{ref}})\)?

questions.title: How does DPO remain consistent when preference data are off-policy relative to \(\pi_{\text{ref}}\)?
questions.question_body: DPO requires \(\pi_{\text{ref}}\) because the loss uses \(\log \pi_\theta(y)/\pi_{\text{ref}}(y)\). But realistic preference datasets might come from an earlier SFT model or a different generator. The paper suggests re-fitting \(\pi_{\text{ref}}\) on preferred completions when the original SFT is unavailable. Under what assumptions does this produce a consistent estimator of the optimal policy? How sensitive is DPO to mismatch between the true reference used to generate the pairs and the proxy \(\pi_{\text{ref}}\) used in training?

questions.title: Clarifying the equivalence classes of rewards: why is adding \(f(x)\) inconsequential?
questions.question_body: The theory section defines an equivalence relation where \(r \sim r'\) if \(r(x,y) - r'(x,y) = f(x)\). I understand BT depends only on reward differences, but could someone show explicitly that (a) the BT likelihood is invariant under adding \(f(x)\), and (b) the optimal policy under the KL-regularized objective is also invariant to this transformation via Eq. (5)?

questions.title: Understanding Theorem 1: does the DPO reparameterization cover all BT-consistent reward classes?
questions.question_body: Theorem 1 claims that any reward class consistent with Plackett–Luce/BT can be represented as \(r(x,y)=\beta\log\frac{\pi(y\mid x)}{\pi_{\text{ref}}(y\mid x)}\) for some \(\pi\). Could someone restate the key assumptions (“mild assumptions”) and give an intuitive proof sketch? In particular, how does the projection via the partition function ensure the resulting \(\pi\) is a valid policy (nonnegative and sums to 1) for all \(x\)?

questions.title: How does DPO extend to Plackett–Luce with k-way rankings, not just pairwise preferences?
questions.question_body: Appendix C says the derivation extends to Plackett–Luce models. If I have a ranked list \(y_{(1)} \succ y_{(2)} \succ \dots \succ y_{(k)}\) for a given \(x\), what is the explicit DPO loss analogous to Eq. (8)? Does it become a sum over terms like \(\log \sigma\big(\beta(\log \pi(y_{(i)})/\pi_{\text{ref}}(y_{(i)}) - \log \pi(y_{(j)})/\pi_{\text{ref}}(y_{(j)}))\big)\) for pairs, or is there a more direct factorized form?

questions.title: Control-as-inference perspective: why this direction of KL and what would change if reversed?
questions.question_body: Eq. (10) frames actor optimization as minimizing \(\mathbb{D}_{\mathrm{KL}}[\pi_\theta \| \pi^*]\). Why choose this KL direction rather than \(\mathbb{D}_{\mathrm{KL}}[\pi^* \| \pi_\theta]\)? What properties (mode covering vs mode seeking) matter here for text generation, and how does DPO’s reparameterization relate to the chosen KL direction?

questions.title: Why does DPO not need a learned value baseline while PPO does?
questions.question_body: The paper argues that the normalization term in Eq. (10), \(\beta \log \sum_y \pi_{\text{ref}}(y\mid x) \exp(r_\phi/\beta)\), acts like a soft value baseline and is important for variance reduction in actor-critic. How does the DPO change-of-variables eliminate the need for this baseline entirely? Is there an implicit baseline embedded in the log-ratio form?

questions.title: How is the KL constraint actually enforced in DPO if we never sample on-policy during training?
questions.question_body: In PPO-RLHF, you explicitly target a KL to the reference and adjust updates via clipping. In DPO, the training is purely supervised on the offline preference pairs with a log-ratio term. Does minimizing Eq. (8) guarantee a certain KL to \(\pi_{\text{ref}}\) at convergence, or is \(\beta\) only indirectly controlling the tradeoff? How should we monitor and calibrate the achieved KL during/after training?

questions.title: Practical computation of log-probabilities for DPO with sampling tricks (top-p, top-k, temperature)
questions.question_body: At inference time, we often sample with temperature, top-p, or top-k truncation. But DPO’s training uses log-probabilities \(\log \pi_\theta(y \mid x)\) and \(\log \pi_{\text{ref}}(y \mid x)\) under the full model distribution. If the preference dataset was generated under a truncated sampler, should we compute log-probs with the truncated distribution or with the base softmax? Does this mismatch bias the DPO objective?

questions.title: Does DPO require on-policy preference data, or can it learn from arbitrary offline pairs?
questions.question_body: The DPO loss treats the observed pairs as i.i.d. samples from the BT model. If the pairs come from very different generators (e.g., mixtures of several LMs across training), is the estimator still consistent for the putative \(\pi^*\)? Are there known failure modes if the data distribution is heavily biased (e.g., lots of near-duplicates or only very easy wins)?

questions.title: Clarifying the relationship between DPO and “Best-of-N with a learned reward”
questions.question_body: Experimentally, Best-of-\(N\) with a learned reward can be strong but computationally heavy at inference. Since DPO directly optimizes a policy that is optimal for an implicit reward, is there a theoretical reason to expect DPO to approach the performance of Best-of-\(N\) as data increases? Or are there cases where the learned reward’s ranking quality is good but the DPO policy still cannot match Best-of-\(N\) due to distributional constraints to \(\pi_{\text{ref}}\)?

questions.title: What are the concrete failure modes of DPO and how can we detect them during training?
questions.question_body: The paper mentions potential degeneration with a naive objective and hints at over-optimization questions. In practice, what signs indicate DPO is failing (e.g., toxic mode collapse, excessive verbosity, reward hacking relative to a proxy)? Are there diagnostics beyond tracking the KL to \(\pi_{\text{ref}}\), such as monitoring entropy, calibration of win-probabilities, or the margin \(\hat r_\theta(y_w) - \hat r_\theta(y_l)\)?

questions.title: Extending DPO to continuous control or other modalities: what changes in the derivation?
questions.question_body: The derivation relies on log-ratios of densities and cancellation of a partition function when using BT/Plackett–Luce. If we consider continuous actions (e.g., diffusion models for images, or continuous control), what are the key steps that still go through, and where do we need new assumptions (e.g., absolute continuity of \(\pi\) w.r.t. \(\pi_{\text{ref}}\), handling of measure-zero events)?

questions.title: Do we need to normalize rewards to zero mean for DPO like in standard RM training?
questions.question_body: In reward model training it is common to center the rewards so that \(\mathbb{E}[r(x,y)]=0\) per \(x\) to reduce variance. Since DPO’s implicit reward is a log-probability ratio, its mean is not explicitly controlled. Is there any benefit to normalizing or centering the implicit rewards during training (e.g., by subtracting a per-prompt baseline), or would that break the equivalence that makes DPO work?
